papers.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
papers.authors: Kaidi Fu, Xu-Hao Lu, Pingwei Sun, Jianchao Tan, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
papers.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In p
papers.summary: In MoE inference, expert parallelism makes every layer wait for the busiest rank. Prefill is compute-bound, so the bottleneck is the token count on that rank; at moderate batch sizes, decode is memory-bound, and the bottleneck becomes how many experts are active on each rank. Even if training used load balancing, a frozen router at serving time still sees batch variation and domain drift, and what stalls latency is the instantaneous load on each rank. RankCast keeps each token's predicted top experts and assigns the remaining slots from a larger candidate set to lighter ranks: it steers flexible work toward less loaded ranks in prefill, and closes some experts on the busiest ranks in decode. The extra kernels can overlap with model execution. On Qwen3-235B and Qwen3.5-397B, it removes more than 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, raises prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and cuts decode time per output token by up to 10%, with a quality cost below one percentage point.

papers.title: PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xiaoqiang Guo, Yifan Lin, Yang Liu, Jianan Zhang, Yingqi Peng, Jiamei Lv, Yi Gao, Wei Dong
papers.abstract: Pipeline parallelism can serve long-context language models on PCIe servers and across heterogeneous GPU clusters. Existing engines split prefill into token chunks to limit decode stalls. The chunk size also sets the GPU batch width and the size of activation transfers between stages. Small chunks reload model weights more often. Large chunks can keep the GPU and the link busy long enough to delay interactive requests. PipeAxes runs wide prefill batches a few layers at a time so decodes can run between slices. A fused Triton Hadamard-INT4 codec compresses activations, which travel in independently sized row groups over parallel TCP sockets. The scheduler uses latency slack to choose batch width, slice depth, and row-group size. We evaluated PipeAxes in 97 replays covering 5,016 requests on A800, RTX 4090, and RTX 3090 GPUs. All 74 requests met their latency targets during a tenfold bandwidth swing. In a four-stage mixture-of-experts pipeline, PipeAxes served requests within their laten
papers.summary: When pipeline parallelism serves long-context models on PCIe servers or heterogeneous GPUs, existing engines often split prefill into token chunks, and that chunk size also sets the GPU batch width and the size of activation transfers between stages. Small chunks reload weights too often, while large chunks can stall interactive requests. PipeAxes runs wide prefill batches a few layers at a time so decodes can slip in between slices, sends compressed activations in independently sized row groups, and uses latency slack to choose batch width, slice depth, and row-group size. The measure of success is how many requests meet time-to-first-token, time-per-output-token, and tail-interval targets together. In a four-stage MoE pipeline, it serves requests within their latency targets at 23.3 times the rate of calibrated Revisit-PP. In a mixed long-context workload, high-percentile time to first token for short requests fell from 129.8 seconds with native vLLM to 512 milliseconds.

papers.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
papers.authors: Hoonki Lee, Haechan Shin, Hyuntaek Jung, Yeonu Choi, Sangyeob Kim
papers.abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR
papers.summary: On-device deployment often has to switch precision under changing memory and energy budgets, but if a single checkpoint can only be read at integer bit widths, the gaps between adjacent precisions stay large and accuracy drops sharply at two bits. When several precisions share leading bit-planes while chasing different targets, they often lose still more accuracy. Any-Rate serves many precisions from one checkpoint, from two to eight bits, with half-bit steps between two and four bits. It restricts some bit-planes to short codewords, shares one lookup table per row across precisions, and encodes each precision against its own target, which reduces the loss from sharing leading planes. Across four language models, the two-bit mode still keeps 69% of FP16 accuracy, leading other multi-precision methods, and it decodes about as fast as existing kernels. An LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy.

papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.authors: Hong Liu, Rui Cen, Junhan Shi, Lin Niu, Runzhi Fan, Zhaojing Zhou, Haodi Lei, Jiebin Zhang, Saiyong Yang, Junqiang Zheng, Zhenghai Xue, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu
papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it s
papers.summary: Natively sparse long-context models already select positions for each target query, yet speculative drafters still often keep their own context cache, or else read the whole prompt or a recent window. A private cache costs memory, slows prefill, and crowds out concurrency, and computing a fresh selection per query would grow with context length. DFly2 reuses the cache and the selection the target has already paid for: each draft layer reads only the positions its paired target layer cached and its indexer chose, and it runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. The selection stays a fixed size but can land anywhere in the context, so a long prompt does not mean a larger read. At high concurrency and matched per-user decode speed, it delivers 62% and 81% more throughput on long-context and agentic sets when serving DS-V4.1-Flash.

papers.title: How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling
papers.abstract: Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models, where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and...
papers.summary: When serving world models, long sequences often make attention a clear bottleneck. On NVIDIA RTX Blackwell, NVFP4 can raise throughput with four-bit matrix multiplies, but dependencies among softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage can leave Tensor Cores idle. On these consumer cards, attention is often bound by matrix multiplies rather than by softmax. A register-recycling schedule splits each score tile into two narrower slots and, after softmax quantization, immediately reuses the registers for the next tile's work, so the kernel need not allocate a second full score buffer. Registers are nearly full, so there is little room to hold a second score tile at the same time. On an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, this speeds up the NVFP4 attention kernel by up to 1.64 times. Reactor integrated the optimized kernel into its production serving stack for world models, cutting end-to-end inference latency by up to 15.34% on workloads such as LongLive, Helios, OmniDreams, and Cosmos 3 Nano. The schedule has been merged into the FlashInfer main branch.

papers.title: Asymmetric Speculative Decoding: Unlocking In-Context Learning in Draft Models
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding addresses Large Language Model (LLM) inference latency by first drafting and then verifying in parallel. Yet practical speedups fall far short of theoretical bounds, especially on reasoning tasks. We identify the root cause as task isomorphism: existing methods provide identical prompts to both models, forcing the draft model to solve problems beyond its capacity. This produces high rejection rates that eliminate parallelization gains. We discover that acceptance rates increase monotonically during generation, revealing a latent in-context learning (ICL) effect wherein the draft model progressively aligns with the target distribution by learning from verified tokens. Controlled experiments with varying context window sizes confirm this improvement stems from ICL-driven alignment rather than token difficulty. Motivated by this finding, we propose Asymmetric Speculative Decoding (AsymSpec), a training-free framework that decouples the prompts provided to draft and ta
papers.summary: Practical speedups from speculative decoding often fall far short of theoretical bounds, especially on reasoning tasks. The usual cause is that the draft and target models receive the same prompt, so a much weaker drafter is forced to solve the problem itself, and high rejection rates wipe out the benefit of parallel verification. Even when the drafter reaches a correct answer, it may get there by a trajectory the target rejects. Acceptance rates rise steadily during generation, which shows that the drafter is doing in-context learning from already verified tokens and gradually aligning with the target distribution. AsymSpec stops giving both sides the same prompt: it supplies the drafter with task-relevant worked solutions, so the job becomes simulation rather than problem solving, and it needs no retraining. On reasoning, code generation, and summarization, it speeds up autoregressive decoding by 2.29 to 4.95 times and also outperforms standard speculative decoding.

papers.title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
papers.authors: Ayhan Suleymanzade, Sean McLeish, Sehoon Kim, Jinwoo Kim, Antoine Bosselut
papers.abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training o
papers.summary: Looped language models can change how much computation they spend on a token by adjusting the number of loops, without a matching increase in unique parameters. Shallow loops are often used as a fast drafter, with deep loops as the verifier, because drafting still uses the full set of parameters. Those shallow loops can also predict several future tokens at once. Floodgates appends a block of mask tokens at the end of the sequence and, with a low-rank adaptation, learns to draft those positions in parallel, while remaining lossless. The speedup also depends on training the looped model at all depths, so the shallow drafter can use the deep prefix cache already computed during verification. Across seven models, five benchmarks, and a range of batch sizes and decoding modes, it is the fastest lossless method in most cases, reaching up to 7.5 times speedup. On shallow four-loop models, a single drafting loop is up to 5.1 times faster on average; the higher figure appears on deeper models with elastic drafting.

papers.title: Libtt: A Compiler and Runtime for Tenstorrent Processors
papers.abstract: Libtt brings the PyTorch and JAX ecosystem to Tenstorrent hardware. It implements PJRT, the interface through which XLA-based frameworks drive Google's TPUs, so JAX runs on it directly, PyTorch runs through TorchTPU, and software written for TPUs carries over with no changes except replacing custom kernels. Built on Tenstorrent's open-source compiler and runtime, libtt ships the entire stack, from the compiler to the multi-chip runtime, as a single shared library. It contains extensive fixes to the upstream Tenstorrent software to make existing PyTorch and JAX code work out of the box, and extensive new compiler optimizations to make it fast. It passes most of the JAX and TorchTPU test suites and runs SGLang, TorchTitan, and Miles, covering serving, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
papers.summary: Running existing PyTorch and JAX programs on Tenstorrent chips depends on speaking the same interface those frameworks already use to drive TPUs. Libtt implements that interface, so JAX runs directly, PyTorch runs through TorchTPU, and software written for TPUs carries over with no changes except replacing custom kernels. It ships the compiler and the multi-chip runtime as one shared library, fixes many upstream issues, and adds compiler optimizations so existing code is more likely to run out of the box. It passes most of the JAX and TorchTPU test suites and runs SGLang, TorchTitan, and Miles, covering serving, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. On four chips, it can follow TorchTitan's TPU training path without changing the trainer's source. In small checks, starting losses on the chips agree with a CPU run to three decimal digits. With fused attention and a fused loss, training throughput for Qwen3-8B rose from 287 to 435 tokens per second per chip.

papers.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
papers.authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, model-driven context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~rightarrow~56\%), and Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that inference engines can make model-
papers.summary: Today's agent harnesses usually manage context for the model: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. The alternative is to let the model decide, through a context API, when and what to compact. The comparison was run in NOOA, NVIDIA's open-source agent harness, on document research and machine-learning engineering tasks, with context budgets from tight to very wide. Models that use the API well reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially under tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score on OfficeQA Pro v2, from 21% to 56%. Models differ widely in how often they call the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start, and prompt changes shift that timing. If an inference engine reuses the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, prefill compute per request falls by up to 15%, with no measurable change in accuracy.

papers.title: nnTrace: Detecting and Localizing Silent Bugs in Distributed Training
papers.authors: Haitian Jiang, Shaowei Zhu, Zhen Zhang, Zhenyu Song, Xinwei Fu, Zhen Jia, Yida Wang, Jinyang Li
papers.abstract:
Distributed training is essential for scaling LLM training across thousands of GPUs. However, as distributed training requires complex implementations, they are prone to silent bugs, which do not produce explicit error signals but lead to in correct training outcomes. Common debugging practices based on monitoring training loss or gradient norm curves are slow or unable to detect bugs and also do not help localize bugs.

We design and implement nnTrace, the first systematic differential testing system for detecting and localizing silent bugs in distributed training. nnTrace aligns intermediate tensors from distributed training with those from a trusted reference implementation. To properly compare the floating-point values in the corresponding tensors, we propose a novel mathematical analysis that provides a guideline for setting tolerances, enabling nnTrace to distinguish bug-induced errors from numerical errors. Experimental results demonstrate that nnTrace effectively detects 11 exi
papers.summary: Distributed training spreads work across thousands of GPUs, and as the implementation gets more complex, it becomes prone to silent bugs that raise no explicit error yet still produce incorrect training outcomes. Watching the training-loss or gradient-norm curve is often slow, sometimes misses the bug entirely, and does little to localize it. nnTrace detects and localizes these bugs with differential testing: it aligns intermediate tensors from distributed training with those from a trusted reference implementation, then compares the floating-point values in corresponding tensors. The tolerance cannot be set arbitrarily; a mathematical analysis provides a guideline that separates bug-induced errors from ordinary numerical error. That way, a check is less likely to treat rounding differences as bugs, or to let a truly silent fault slip through. For people training at scale, being able to point to the layer or tensor that went wrong is much more useful than noticing only that a curve later looks off.

scenario: Today's infrastructure papers ask how serving can wait less on the busiest rank, and how prefill chunk size can stop dictating both compute and communication. Another line makes speculative drafters cheaper, or lets the drafter read worked examples and simulate the target instead of solving the same hard problem. Others let the model decide when to compact its own context, or bring the existing PyTorch and JAX stack to Tenstorrent chips. Some systems balance expert parallelism with different objectives in prefill and decode, some cut energy by serving many precisions, including half-bit steps, from one checkpoint, and some speed up low-bit attention on consumer GPUs by recycling registers. Silent bugs in distributed training are being hunted by aligning intermediate tensors, rather than by watching the loss curve alone.
